meta.blurb: Margaret Hale leaves the green villages of southern England for the smoky mill town of Milton, where she clashes with proud mill owner John Thornton. Strikes, secrets and sorrow force both to question what they believe. Can north and south ever understand each other?
meta.bible: Margaret Hale: the heroine, eighteen at the start, honest, brave and a little proud; she grew up in the south. Mr Hale: her father, a gentle clergyman who leaves the church over matters of conscience and becomes a private tutor. Mrs Hale: her mother, delicate and sad to leave the south; she dies in Milton. Frederick Hale: Margaret's brother, a sailor who took part in a mutiny against a cruel captain and lives in exile abroad. John Thornton: a Milton cotton mill owner, strong, serious and proud; he rose from poverty. Hannah Thornton: his strict, devoted mother. Fanny Thornton: his younger sister. Nicholas Higgins: a mill worker and union man, honest and stubborn. Bessy Higgins: his daughter, who is dying of lung disease from cotton dust. Boucher: a striker whose death leaves his children alone. Mr Bell: Mr Hale's old friend from Oxford, Margaret's godfather and landlord of Marlborough Mills; he dies and leaves Margaret his fortune. Mrs Shaw: Margaret's aunt, who lives in London. Edith Lennox: Margaret's cousin, who marries Captain Lennox. Captain Lennox: Edith's husband. Henry Lennox: the captain's brother, a lawyer; he proposes to Margaret and is refused. Dixon: the Hales' faithful servant. Leonards: the man who tries to arrest Frederick at the station and falls. Helstone: the quiet southern village where the Hales live at first. Milton: the northern mill town, based on Manchester, full of smoke and noise. Marlborough Mills: Thornton's cotton mill. Harley Street: Mrs Shaw's London house. Oxford: where Mr Hale dies. Spain: where Frederick lives. England. Author: Elizabeth Gaskell, published 1854 to 1855. Voice and tone: serious, warm and social-minded; a love story set against a strike; deaths are stated plainly, with no gore; the ending is hopeful.

A1A2: Margaret Hale lived in London with her aunt and her pretty cousin.
A lawyer asked Margaret to marry him, but she said no.
At home in Helstone, her father said he must leave the church.
They had to leave their lovely village and move to a northern town.
Milton was a big town full of smoke, noise and busy mills.
Margaret's mother was sick, and the new house felt small and dark.
Mr Thornton, a rich mill owner, came to study with her father.
Margaret visited the mill and met Mr Thornton's strict, proud mother.
Margaret met Bessy Higgins, a young factory girl who was very sick.
Bessy's father, Nicholas, was a poor worker who talked bravely about his rights.
Mr Thornton had been poor as a boy, so he worked very hard.
At a big dinner, mill owners said workers must do as they were told.
Margaret told Mr Thornton he was too hard on his workers, and they argued.
Margaret's mother secretly wanted to see her son Frederick, who had to live far away.
The workers wanted more money, so they stopped work, and the mills closed.
Mr Thornton brought in new workers from Ireland, and the town became angry.
An angry crowd came to Mr Thornton's house, and Margaret ran to help him.
She stood in front of him, and a stone hit her head.
Next day Mr Thornton asked her to marry him, but she said no.
Margaret felt ashamed, and she could not stop thinking about him.
Bessy died quietly, and Margaret stayed with her family in their sadness.
Margaret's mother was dying, and she asked Margaret to send for Frederick.
Frederick came secretly at night, and his mother was very happy to see him.
At the station, a man tried to stop Frederick, but he fell badly.
Mr Thornton saw Margaret walking with a young man late in the evening.
Margaret's mother died, and Frederick said goodbye and left the country again.
The police asked Margaret about the station, and she lied to protect her brother.
Mr Thornton heard her lie and kept quiet, but he thought badly of her.
Higgins's friend died in the river, and Higgins took care of his children.
Higgins asked Mr Thornton for work, and Thornton gave him a job.
The two men talked together and slowly began to understand each other.
Mr Hale went to Oxford to see his old friend Mr Bell.
There Mr Hale died suddenly, and Margaret was left without a mother or father.
Margaret went to London and lived with her aunt, wearing black clothes.
In London she had everything she needed, but she missed Milton.
Meanwhile, Mr Thornton's business was weak, and he lost a lot of money.
Mr Bell, Margaret's godfather, wanted to visit Helstone once more with her.
Helstone was different now, and Margaret felt sad about the changes.
Mr Bell died, and he left all his money to Margaret.
Now Margaret was rich, and she heard that Mr Thornton was in trouble.
Mr Thornton's mill closed, because he could not pay what he owed.
A friend told Mr Thornton the truth about the young man at the station.
Thornton felt sorry, because Margaret had been protecting her brother all that time.
He came to London, and they met in her aunt's house, nervous and shy.
Thornton said he had to leave Milton, and he thanked her for helping Higgins.
Margaret said her money was sleeping, and she wanted to use it well.
Thornton was proud, but he listened to her plan and accepted it.
Then he asked if she could ever love him, and she smiled.
She said yes, and they held hands and promised to marry.
Together they saved the mill, and the north and the south became friends.
B1B2: Margaret Hale, eighteen years old, has lived in London with her aunt Mrs Shaw and her cousin Edith. Now Edith is about to marry Captain Lennox, and Margaret is going home to Helstone, the quiet village she loves.
At Helstone, Henry Lennox, the captain's brother, visits and asks Margaret to marry him. She likes him as a friend, but she does not love him, so she says no.
Margaret's father, Mr Hale, is the village clergyman, and the family lives happily in the countryside. One day he tells his daughter that he has doubts about the church and must leave it.
Mr Hale decides to move the family to Milton, a manufacturing town in the north. Margaret packs up the home she has always known, and her mother weeps at leaving the green fields behind.
Milton is nothing like the south, because the air is thick with smoke and the streets echo with noise. Margaret looks at the crowds of workers hurrying to the mills, and she feels very far from home.
The Hales rent a small house, and Mr Hale begins to earn money as a private teacher. Mrs Hale grows weaker every week, and Margaret worries about her more than she admits.
One of her father's pupils is Mr Thornton, a tall, serious man who owns a cotton mill. He is polite, but Margaret thinks he is proud and hard, and he thinks she is cold and haughty.

Margaret visits Marlborough Mills and meets Mr Thornton's mother, Hannah Thornton, a strong and strict woman. Mrs Thornton does not hide the fact that she thinks Margaret is too proud to understand northern ways.
In the street Margaret meets a thin young mill girl called Bessy Higgins, who coughs badly. Bessy tells her that cotton dust has filled her lungs, and Margaret promises to visit her.

Bessy's father, Nicholas Higgins, is a proud workman who believes that workers should stand together against their masters. Margaret likes his honesty, and they begin to argue and learn from each other.
One evening Mr Thornton tells Margaret and her father how he rose from poverty. After his father's death, he worked as a boy to feed his mother and sister, and he has never forgotten that time.
Mr Thornton invites the Hales to a dinner with other mill owners. The men say they have the right to run their mills as they wish, and that workers must simply obey.
Margaret cannot keep silent and tells Mr Thornton that he is too hard on his workers. They argue sharply, but both of them are surprised to find that they enjoy being challenged.

Margaret keeps a family secret that she shares with nobody in Milton. Her brother Frederick, a sailor, took part in a mutiny against a cruel captain, and he cannot return to England without risking his life.
The workers in Milton want better pay, and when the masters refuse, a strike begins. Thousands of people stop working, and soon the whole town is full of anger and hunger.
To keep his mill running, Mr Thornton decides to bring in workers from Ireland. The strikers see this as a betrayal, and Higgins warns Margaret that trouble is coming.
One day an angry crowd gathers outside Mr Thornton's house, shouting and throwing stones. Margaret, who is visiting, begs him to speak to them, because she is sure that he can calm them.
When the mob breaks through the gate, Margaret throws her arms around Mr Thornton to protect him. A sharp stone strikes her forehead, and the crowd, shocked, falls silent and drifts away.

The next morning Mr Thornton calls on Margaret and asks her to marry him, because he thinks she must care for him. She refuses coldly and says she would have protected anyone, and he leaves hurt and angry.
After he goes, Margaret is ashamed of the way she spoke, and she cannot stop thinking about him. Meanwhile the strike collapses, because the workers are too hungry to hold out any longer.
Bessy grows weaker, and one evening she dies, with Margaret at her side. Higgins, who is heartbroken, begins to trust Margaret as a friend, and she helps his family in whatever way she can.
Mrs Hale is now very ill, and she begs to see her son once more before she dies. Margaret writes to Frederick in Spain, even though she knows how dangerous the journey will be.
Frederick comes secretly by night, and his mother is overjoyed to hold him again. For a few days the little house is filled with happiness, although the family fears being discovered.

On the last evening, Margaret walks with her brother to the station, and a man who once knew him tries to arrest him. They struggle, the man falls hard onto the ground, and Frederick runs for the train.
Mr Thornton happens to be at the station that evening and sees Margaret with a young man. He does not know who the stranger is, and a cold fear grows in his heart.
Soon afterwards Mrs Hale dies peacefully, with her children beside her. Frederick must leave quickly before he is recognised, and Margaret is left to comfort her grieving father.
The man from the station dies of his injuries, and the police begin to ask questions. Margaret is asked whether she was there, and she says no, because she must protect her brother.
Mr Thornton is the magistrate who hears her answer, and he knows that she is lying. He says nothing to help or to harm her, but he now believes that she has a secret sweetheart.

Margaret feels deeply ashamed, because she has never told a lie before. In the days that follow, she hears that a man named Boucher has been found drowned, leaving his children with no one to feed them.
Higgins takes in Boucher's children and feeds them, although he has little for himself. Then, to support them, he goes to Mr Thornton's gates and humbly asks for work.
Mr Thornton hesitates, because Higgins led the strike, but he sees the man's honesty and gives him a job. In time the two men talk openly, and Thornton starts a cheap kitchen for his workers.
Mr Hale's old friend and Margaret's godfather, Mr Bell, visits Milton. He invites Mr Hale to come back to Oxford with him, and Mr Hale, who longs for books and old friends, agrees.
In Oxford Mr Hale dies suddenly in his sleep, a few days after arriving. Margaret travels there with a heavy heart, and she is now alone in the world except for her brother and her aunt.
Margaret leaves Milton and moves to London to live with her aunt, Mrs Shaw. She wears black and sits quietly in the grand house, remembering all she has lost.
Life in London is comfortable and quiet, and her cousin Edith is kind. Yet Margaret finds that her thoughts often go back to Milton, to Higgins, and to a man she cannot forget.
Back in Milton, Mr Thornton's business is in trouble. Trade is bad, and he has taken risks, so his money is slipping away, although he works harder than ever.
Mr Bell is growing old and ill, and he asks Margaret to visit Helstone with him one last time. She agrees at once, for she has often dreamed of the village where she grew up.
At Helstone everything has changed, because the old friends have gone and the village feels smaller. Margaret feels sad, and Mr Bell, who is tired by the journey, falls ill.
Mr Bell dies soon afterwards, and Margaret learns that he has left her all his money. He also owned the mill that Mr Thornton rents, and now that belongs to her.
Margaret is now rich, and she hears, with alarm, that Mr Thornton is close to ruin. She asks her lawyer Henry Lennox for advice, and he is surprised to see how much she cares.
Mr Thornton's mill closes, because he cannot pay his debts. He feels the shame deeply, but he promises that every worker will be paid what he is owed.
In London, Mr Thornton meets Henry Lennox on business and hears the truth about the night at the station. The young man was Margaret's brother, and she lied only to protect him.
Thornton is stunned and full of regret that he doubted her. He understands now that she is brave, and that he judged her unfairly.
He visits Margaret at her aunt's house, dressed formally and speaking politely. She is nervous too, and for a moment neither of them knows how to begin.
Thornton explains that he must leave Milton, and he thanks her for her kindness to Higgins. Margaret says she has heard that he lost his mill, and she is very sorry.
Margaret says that her money is lying idle, and she wants to put it to use. She asks him to take it as a loan, so that he can keep his mill open.
Thornton is proud, and at first he refuses to take help from her. She smiles gently, however, and says that she knows he is a good man of business and that the loan would be safe.
At last he asks whether she will give him more than money, and she lowers her eyes. Her silence tells him the truth, and he takes her hands in his.
Margaret says that she has loved him for a long time, and she will marry him if he will have her. Thornton, filled with joy, kisses her, and the two promise never to let pride separate them again.

The mill reopens, and Higgins works there again, while the masters and the workers learn to listen to each other. Margaret and John Thornton marry, and in their home the north and the south are joined at last.
C1C2: At eighteen, Margaret Hale has spent the greater part of her girlhood in her aunt's elegant house in London, where life is arranged around dinners, calls and the endless chatter of society. Her cousin Edith is about to marry a dashing captain, and the wedding sets the household in a flutter of lace and congratulation. Margaret, who feels more at home among green lanes than drawing rooms, longs to return to her father's quiet parsonage in Helstone.

Back in the village, Margaret is surprised by the visit of Henry Lennox, a young lawyer who is the captain's brother and who has plainly been thinking of her. One afternoon, as they walk together beneath the trees, he declares his love and asks her to marry him. Margaret, who has felt only friendship, refuses him gently and is astonished to find herself relieved.

Life in Helstone is all she could wish: her father is the beloved vicar, her mother is gentle and delicate, and the days pass peacefully among the roses and the hedgerows. Then one evening, Mr Hale confesses that he has been tormented by doubts and can no longer, in conscience, remain a minister of the church. Margaret listens in silence, for she can see that his mind is made up, and that nothing she says will change it.

Mr Hale has decided to move his family to Milton, a great manufacturing town in the north, where he hopes to support them by teaching. The news strikes his wife like a blow, since she cannot imagine life away from the quiet fields where she has spent her married years. Margaret, hiding her own sorrow, takes charge of the packing and bids a long, silent farewell to every corner of the home she loves.

Milton greets them with a sky darkened by smoke and a ceaseless roar of machinery, and the pale, hurrying crowds seem to Margaret like another race of beings. After the sweetness of the southern countryside, the place feels harsh, grimy and unwelcoming. Yet she is struck, in spite of herself, by the energy of the town and by the grim determination in the faces of the people.

The Hales settle into a modest house, and Mr Hale, who has never worked for money before, takes up the unfamiliar task of teaching the sons of the manufacturers. Mrs Hale, worn out by the move and by the city air, takes to her bed and grows weaker with every week. Margaret, who must manage the household with only the faithful Dixon to help her, begins to feel the weight of responsibilities she never expected.

Among her father's pupils is Mr Thornton, a tall, dark and serious mill owner, who has risen by his own efforts and has little time for flattery. Margaret, accustomed to the polished manners of the south, finds him blunt and arrogant, and her cold reception is noticed. He, for his part, concludes that she is a disdainful young lady who looks down on everything that he has worked for.

When Margaret visits Marlborough Mills, she meets Mr Thornton's mother, a formidable widow whose sharp eyes miss nothing and whose devotion to her son is complete. Mrs Thornton regards the southern newcomer with open suspicion, convinced that she has no understanding of the hard-won prosperity of the north. Margaret returns home feeling both humbled and indignant, and wondering what sort of man has such a mother.

Margaret has a chance meeting with Bessy Higgins, a mill worker with a pale face and a hollow cough, who tells her that the fluff of the cotton rooms has settled on her lungs. The young woman speaks of her illness without self-pity, and Margaret, moved by her courage, promises to call on her at home. It is the first sign that, beneath the smoke and clatter of Milton, there is a life that she wants to understand.

Bessy's father, Nicholas Higgins, is a stubborn and clever workman who believes that masters and men will never agree until the men stand united. In his small, spotless kitchen he and Margaret trade opinions with a candour that neither of them has met before, and they soon discover a mutual respect. From these visits Margaret begins to see the quarrel between the classes through the eyes of those who suffer most from it.

One evening Mr Thornton, speaking to Margaret and her father with unexpected openness, recalls the years of his boyhood when his own father's death had left the family destitute. He tells how he worked long hours in a shop to feed his mother and sister, and how every shilling he saved was a victory. Margaret, listening, is forced to admit that the man she judged so harshly has earned his place through hardship and sacrifice.

The Hales are invited to a grand dinner at the Thorntons', where the other mill owners speak with great confidence about their right to manage their own affairs as they see fit. Their talk of hands and wages, as if the workers were so many machines, makes Margaret uncomfortable in her seat. She holds her tongue, but she cannot help noticing how little the men in the room seem to know of those who toil for them.

Later, when she can keep silent no longer, Margaret tells Mr Thornton that he is too severe, and that a master ought to take an interest in the lives of the people who work for him. He answers that the mill is his own business and that kindness cannot replace authority. The two argue fiercely, yet each leaves the encounter with a secret respect for the other's sincerity.

Beneath her calm manner, Margaret carries a secret which she dares not share with anyone in Milton. Her brother Frederick, a naval officer, once joined a mutiny against a tyrannical captain, and since then he has lived abroad as an exile, for England would hang him if he returned. Her mother, wasting away in her sickbed, pines silently for the son she has not seen in many years.

As the weeks pass, discontent grows among the workers, who demand a fair share in the profits that the good times have brought. When the masters refuse to raise wages, the men lay down their tools, and a strike spreads like fire through the mills of Milton. Soon there is hunger in the narrow streets, and anger in the voices that fill them.

Determined to keep production going, Mr Thornton brings a party of Irish labourers into the town, to the fury of the strikers, who see them as traitors and intruders. The streets echo with threats, and Higgins, usually calm, warns Margaret that the town is on the verge of violence. She listens with dread, for she knows that the master's pride will never allow him to give way.

One afternoon, a vast crowd of workers gathers before Mr Thornton's house, shouting abuse and hurling stones through the windows. Margaret, who has come to visit, sees the master standing calmly in the hall and implores him to go out and speak to the people. When he hesitates, she pushes open the door herself and urges him to face them like a man who has nothing to hide.

As the mob surges forward, Margaret flings herself in front of Mr Thornton and wraps her arms about him, hoping that the sight of a woman will shame them into stillness. A sharp stone strikes her on the forehead, and blood runs down her face. The crowd, shocked by what it has done, falls silent and melts away into the dusk.

The next morning, Mr Thornton calls at the Hales' house and, with passionate but clumsy words, asks Margaret to be his wife, believing that her brave act proves her feelings. Margaret, stung by his assumption, replies coldly that she would have defended any man in danger, and that she does not care for him. He leaves wounded to the heart, and she is left troubled by a pain she cannot name.

Once the door has closed, Margaret is ashamed of her harsh reply and cannot understand why his hurt look affects her so deeply. Meanwhile, the strike drags on and finally collapses, for the men can no longer feed their families and have been forced to give in. Higgins, thin and defeated, returns to his work with a bitterness that few can bear to see.

Bessy's strength fades with the autumn, and at last she dies peacefully, with Margaret holding her hand and speaking softly of a better world. Her father, who has always scorned comfort, weeps openly beside the bed, and the grief draws him and Margaret into a lasting friendship. In the weeks that follow, she helps the family in every way she can, and learns the true meaning of loyalty.

At home, Mrs Hale grows rapidly worse, and in her weakness she begs to see her son one last time before she dies. Margaret, terrified of the risk, writes in secret to Frederick, who is living in Spain, and begs him to come at once. The family waits in a state of agonised hope, since they know that his return could mean his arrest.

Frederick arrives by night, wearing a plain disguise, and the reunion between mother and son is so tender that Margaret can hardly bear to watch. For three precious days, the house is filled with talk and laughter, and Mrs Hale seems almost to recover. Yet each knock at the door makes the family start, for they know that a single wrong glance might destroy him.

On the last evening, Margaret walks with her brother to the railway station, where a man who once knew him recognises him and tries to seize him. In the struggle, the man falls heavily from the platform, and Frederick takes his chance, leaps into the carriage and is gone. Margaret, shaking in the lamplight, is left alone with her secret and the sound of the departing train.

As chance would have it, Mr Thornton is passing the station at that very moment, and he catches sight of Margaret in the lamplight beside a young man. He does not know that this is her brother, and the sight tears at his heart, for he has not stopped loving her. Cold with jealousy, he walks away in silence, convinced that she has given herself to another.

A few days later, Mrs Hale dies peacefully in her sleep, having at last seen the son she longed for. Frederick, fearing capture, has already left England, and the family is left to mourn without him. Margaret, with her own grief pressing upon her, turns her attention to her father, who is crushed by the loss.

The man who fell at the station later dies of his injuries, and the police begin to enquire who was with him that night. When an inspector questions Margaret, she looks him in the eye and denies that she was there, knowing that the truth would send her brother to the gallows. It is the first lie of her life, and it sits upon her conscience like a stone.

By ill luck, Mr Thornton is the magistrate present when she gives her false answer, and he knows at once, from what he has seen, that she is not telling the truth. He keeps his silence and does nothing to harm her, although he cannot hide his sorrow at what he believes he has learned. Margaret feels his eyes upon her and burns with a shame she cannot explain.

In the following days the news spreads that a poor striker named Boucher has been found drowned in the river, leaving his children without anyone to care for them. Higgins, though he has little to spare, takes the orphans into his own cottage and feeds them. Margaret, who sees his quiet kindness, is moved to find such goodness in so poor a house.

Weighed down by the extra mouths, Higgins swallows his pride and goes to Mr Thornton's gate to ask humbly for a job. The master, who had once regarded him as an enemy, hesitates for a moment, and then, to the astonishment of his foreman, offers him a place at the mill. It is a small act that opens a new chapter in the relation of master and man.

Over the weeks that follow, Thornton and Higgins begin to talk with a frankness that neither could have imagined before the strike. The master learns what his workers think and want, and he sets up a cheap kitchen where they can buy a hot meal each day. Margaret, hearing of it from Higgins, begins to see that pride and kindness can live in the same man.

Mr Bell, Mr Hale's old friend from Oxford and Margaret's godfather, comes to Milton and finds the clergyman worn and sad. He persuades him to visit the old university, where he might enjoy the books and conversation of earlier years. Mr Hale, longing for a place where his scholarly mind is at home, packs his bag with a happy heart and sets out for Oxford.

In Oxford, within a few days of his arrival, Mr Hale is found dead in his chair, having passed away quietly in his sleep. Margaret, who has hurried south, arrives to find that she has lost her last parent and is quite alone in the world. She weeps for him with a sorrow that seems to go through her whole life.

Having no one left in Milton, Margaret goes to live with her aunt, Mrs Shaw, in the great house in London. She dresses in black, speaks little, and sits for hours at the window, going over the memories of all that she has lost. The grand rooms and the kind cousins around her cannot warm the cold place in her heart.

Life in London is easy and comfortable, and her cousin Edith, who has become a mother, is eager to make her happy. Yet Margaret finds that her thoughts turn constantly northward, to the smoke and clamour of Milton, and to the faces of the people she has known. She is startled to discover that, of all the places she has lived in, that grimy town has left the deepest mark.

In Milton, meanwhile, Mr Thornton's fortunes begin to fall, for trade has slackened and his bold speculations have turned against him. He works longer hours than any of his men, and yet each week he sees his money slip further away. His mother, who has no patience with failure, watches him with a mixture of pride and fear.

Mr Bell, now elderly and frail, asks Margaret to accompany him on a visit to Helstone, a place he loved in his youth. She agrees at once, for the idea of seeing her old home again fills her with a nostalgia she can scarcely control. Together they set out through the green southern countryside, talking quietly of the past.

At Helstone, everything has changed: the old neighbours have moved on, and the lanes that Margaret remembered so fondly seem smaller and plainer than before. She stands beneath her favourite tree and realises that the place she has pined for belongs to a childhood that is gone. Meanwhile, Mr Bell, exhausted by the journey, falls ill, and Margaret nurses him with all the patience she can.

Mr Bell dies a few days later, and Margaret learns that he has left her his entire fortune, together with the mill premises that Mr Thornton rents. She is now a wealthy young woman, although the news brings her little pleasure at a time of mourning. She has become, without knowing it, the landlord of the man she once refused.

As her new wealth settles upon her, Margaret hears of Mr Thornton's difficulties and is alarmed to think of the proud man so close to ruin. She consults her lawyer, Henry Lennox, who is surprised by the warmth with which she asks about the mill. His sharp eyes catch the flush on her cheeks, and he wonders what lies behind it.

Despite his efforts, Mr Thornton cannot meet his debts, and the great mill is forced to close its gates. He feels the shame of it deeply, though he vows that every workman shall be paid in full before he leaves. Even in ruin, he carries himself with the dignity that Margaret had once mistaken for pride.

Business takes Mr Thornton to London, where he meets Henry Lennox and learns, to his amazement, the truth of the night at the station. The young man beside Margaret was her brother Frederick, and she lied to the police only to save his life. Thornton stands silent for a long moment, struck by the knowledge of how much she has suffered in secret.

He is filled with remorse for having thought so ill of her, and he sees now that her courage matches his own. All the cold judgments that he had formed in his pride fall away, leaving only a fierce longing to see her again. He sets off for her aunt's house with a heart full of humility and hope.

In the drawing-room of the house in London, he finds Margaret changed by grief, and more beautiful than he remembers. They greet one another with formal politeness, and each is so conscious of the past that they hardly know how to begin. The room seems filled with things unsaid, and the clock ticks loudly in the silence.

Thornton explains stiffly that he must leave Milton, having lost his mill, and that he has called to thank her for her kindness to Higgins and his family. Margaret tells him gently that she has already heard of his troubles and is truly sorry. He bows his head, and for the first time she sees that his pride can bend.

Collecting her courage, Margaret explains that her fortune lies idle and that she would like to see it put to good use. She suggests that he should borrow it, so that he may keep his mill running and his workers employed. The offer is so sensible and so generous that he cannot at first think of a reply.

Thornton, who has never taken help from anyone, hesitates, for his pride rebels against owing so much to the woman he once asked for love. Margaret, smiling a little, reminds him that he is the shrewdest businessman she knows and that the loan will be perfectly safe. His resistance gives way, and he accepts, though he is conscious that something far greater hangs in the balance.

At last, scarcely able to speak, he asks whether she could ever be persuaded to give him more than money, and Margaret lowers her eyes. In the long silence that follows, he reads in her face an answer that no words could improve upon. He takes her hands in his, and all the stiffness and shyness that has stood between them for so long melts quietly away.

Margaret tells him that she has loved him for a long time, and that she will gladly marry him if he will still have her. Thornton, overcome with joy, draws her towards him and kisses her, and the two promise each other that pride shall never again keep them apart. Outside, the London afternoon goes on as usual, but neither of them hears anything beyond the other's voice.

Under Margaret's new partnership, the mill reopens, Higgins returns to his place, and masters and workers begin to listen to one another. John Thornton and Margaret marry, and in their home the north and the south, the stern and the gentle, are joined at last. The story ends on a note of hope that people of different worlds can, with patience and honesty, learn to understand one another.
